title: Sex-Dependent Impact of Low-Level Lead Exposure during Prenatal Period on Child Psychomotor Functions.
ehr_evidence: This prospective cohort was created in 2007 to evaluate pre- and postnatal exposure to the factors related to the environment and lifestyle, and their impact on outcomes of pregnancy, as well as health status and neurodevelopment of the children; blood lead levels were measured by ICP-MS and neurodevelopment by the Bayley Scales, with data collected via midwife visits, questionnaires, and biological samples rather than EHR.
summary: A prospective mother-child cohort (REPRO_PL) of 402 children from Poland evaluated the sex-dependent effect of low-level prenatal lead exposure (2nd trimester and cord blood) on cognitive, language, and motor developmental scores up to 24 months of age.
key_findings: No statistically significant impact of prenatal lead exposure on girls' psychomotor development.
Among boys, lower cognitive scores were associated with increasing cord blood lead levels (β = −2.07; 95% CI −4.07 to −0.06; p = 0.04).
Language and motor abilities were not significantly associated with lead exposure in either sex (p > 0.05).
No interaction between 2nd trimester blood lead levels and sex; the cord blood lead level × sex interaction was close to significance (p = 0.1).
captured_features: Bayley cognitive, language, and motor composite scores at 12 and 24 months
Gestational week and birth anthropometric measures
Breastfeeding, number of siblings, day care attendance
Salivary cotinine and environmental tobacco smoke exposure
Geometric mean and geometric standard deviation of lead levels
pathologies_diseases: Neurodevelopmental impairment / reduced cognitive function (psychomotor domain)
population: 402 children from the Polish Mother and Child Cohort (REPRO_PL), Poland; prenatal exposure measured in 2nd trimester and cord blood, with neurodevelopmental assessment up to 24 months of age.
limitations: No measurement of lead levels in the children's own blood (only maternal and cord blood).
Did not account for home environment quality, mother-child relationship, parental roles, or maternal IQ.
Selection bias: sample is representative of an urban Polish population with high SES, not rural or disadvantaged areas.
Lack of measurement of other neurotoxic elements (arsenic, cadmium, mercury) that may act synergistically.
